opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the approximate continuity assumption is basically the claim that AI capabilities will improve fairly smoothly as a function of the inputs we put in, things like compute and R&D effort. We're not expecting some sudden discontinuous jump where one day you have a system that's roughly as capable as today's and the next day you have something wildly more powerful with no warning in between.

That shapes our planning a lot, mostly by letting us be more iterative. If progress is roughly continuous, we don't need a complete solution today for every risk a superintelligent system might pose. We can focus on the risks and mitigations relevant to the next generation or two of systems, and expect to see warning signs and intermediate capability levels along the way. That's a big part of why things like dangerous capability evaluations and the Frontier Safety Framework make sense: you test for capabilities, see them start to show up, and put mitigations in place before you cross the threshold where they really matter.

It also means we can study problems empirically on the systems we actually have, rather than reasoning purely in the abstract about some hypothetical future system that looks nothing like today's models. We can use current models as test beds for things like monitoring, interpretability, and amplified oversight, and expect those lessons to carry over reasonably well to slightly more capable systems.

I want to be clear about what it doesn't mean, though. Continuity isn't the same as slow. Our document also takes seriously that we could get very powerful systems on short timelines, plausibly by around 2030, and that AI automating AI research could speed things up a lot. Smooth in terms of inputs can still be very fast in calendar time. So the assumption isn't "we have plenty of time." It's more "there won't be a cliff we can't see coming," which means investing in our ability to notice where we are on the curve and respond quickly.

And if the assumption turned out to be badly wrong, a lot of the iterative approach would be on shakier ground. That's one reason we try to state our assumptions explicitly, so it's clear which parts of the plan depend on them and what we'd need to revisit if the evidence changed.

r001.rationale: Defines the assumption as capabilities improving fairly smoothly with inputs, including compute and R&D effort.

r002.rationale: Says continuity does not mean progress is slow and that smooth progress with inputs can still be very fast in calendar time.

r003.rationale: Says planning can focus on risks and mitigations relevant to the next generation or two of systems and their expected capability levels.

r004.rationale: Does not say inadequate preparedness for anticipated risks could lead to slowing or pausing development.

r005.rationale: Says a complete solution for every risk is not needed today, but does not specifically reject knowing how to align superintelligence as a prerequisite for continued development.

r006.rationale: Does not state that some problems posed by future superintelligence have not yet been identified.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the approximate continuity assumption is one of a handful of core assumptions we laid out in the paper, and honestly it's probably the one doing the most work in determining what we actually plan for.

The basic idea is that we don't expect sudden, discontinuous jumps in capability — no overnight leap from "roughly where we are now" to something wildly superhuman, with nothing in between. Instead, we expect capabilities to improve in a reasonably smooth way as we scale up compute, data, and algorithmic progress. That's not the same as saying progress will be slow. It could be quite fast. But the key thing is that each generation of systems is only modestly more capable than the last, so you're never dealing with something that's a complete black box relative to everything you've seen before.

And that matters enormously for scope, because it means we can rely on a kind of iterative, empirical approach. We get to study the current frontier system, figure out where its failure modes are, develop mitigations, and then test those mitigations on the next system — which is only a bit more capable. The feedback loop stays intact. If instead you had a discontinuity, you'd basically be making a one-shot bet: your safety techniques would have to work the very first time on a system you've never been able to test anything like.

So in practice, the assumption lets us say things like: dangerous capability evaluations are actually useful, because they'll give us warning before a system crosses a threshold rather than after. It lets us say that techniques like amplified oversight — where we use AI to help humans supervise AI — can be bootstrapped, because each step the AI helper is only slightly ahead of where you were last time. And it means we can design the whole framework around things that are testable now, rather than purely theoretical arguments about what a superintelligence would do.

Now, I want to be careful here, because people sometimes hear "continuity" and think we're saying "don't worry, we'll have plenty of time." That's not the claim. If there's a software intelligence explosion — AI automating AI research — you could get a lot of capability in a short calendar period. The continuity assumption is compatible with that. What it rules out is the specific scenario where a single training run produces something categorically different with no precursors. If that happened, I'd say a lot of our plan would be in trouble, and we try to be upfront about that.

The other thing I'd flag is that this assumption is a bet, not a proof. We think it's well-supported by what we've seen so far — scaling laws have been remarkably smooth — but we hold it with some humility. Part of the reason to invest in things like interpretability and more theoretical alignment work is precisely as a hedge: if continuity turns out to be wrong, we want to have some tools that don't depend on it. But as a planning assumption, it's what lets us prioritize concrete, near-term work over indefinitely open-ended research, and I think that's the right call given what we know.

r001.rationale: It describes smooth capability gains as compute, data, and algorithmic progress scale, but does not mention labour or equivalent input.

r002.rationale: It says continuity does not mean progress will be slow and allows for a software intelligence explosion producing rapid gains over a short calendar period.

r003.rationale: It describes planning around current systems and modestly more capable next generations, using evaluations and iterative safety work to address risks as capabilities advance.

r004.rationale: It says a discontinuous jump would put the plan in trouble, but does not present inadequate preparedness for anticipated risks as a reason to slow or pause development.

r005.rationale: It favors concrete near-term work over indefinitely open-ended research, but does not address whether solving ASI alignment is a prerequisite for continued AI development.

r006.rationale: It discusses risks and failure modes, but does not state that some problems posed by future superintelligence have not yet been identified.

astra-6.text:
The rough idea is that the systems we’re going to build next will be sufficiently similar to the systems we have now that studying today’s systems can tell us something useful about how to make those future systems safe. That doesn’t mean capabilities improve smoothly, or that we won’t see surprises. It’s an assumption about how much our understanding and our safety techniques will transfer.

That gives us a tractable scope for planning. We can ask: as these systems become more capable, what would we need in order to evaluate them, train them to behave appropriately, and maintain meaningful oversight? We can do empirical work on those questions now, rather than needing to solve the problem for every possible kind of intelligence.

The limitation is that this is a conditional approach. If we end up building AGI in a way that’s radically different from what we’re studying, some of that work might not apply. So I wouldn’t interpret the assumption as a guarantee that our current approach will work. It’s a working hypothesis that lets us make progress, and something we need to revisit as we get more evidence.

r001.rationale: It defines the assumption in terms of future systems resembling current ones, not AI progress being relatively smooth with respect to compute, labour, or similar inputs.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the assumption does not mean capabilities will improve smoothly.

r003.rationale: It proposes studying safety questions as systems grow more capable, but does not say planning prioritizes problems at the capability levels Google DeepMind expects to reach.

r004.rationale: It says the approach may not apply if AGI differs radically from current systems, but does not mention slowing or pausing development due to inadequate preparedness.

r005.rationale: It says there is no need to solve the problem for every possible kind of intelligence, but does not reject knowing how to align artificial superintelligence as a prerequisite for proceeding.

r006.rationale: It mentions possible surprises and radically different AGI, but does not state that some future superintelligence problems have not yet been identified.

sol-6.1.text:
The rough idea is that the systems we build next will be sufficiently similar to the systems we have now that studying today’s systems can tell us something useful about their risks and how to mitigate them. That doesn’t mean progress will be smooth, or that there won’t be surprising new capabilities. It’s an assumption about how much our evidence will generalise.

That makes the safety work more concrete: we can investigate failure modes, develop evaluations, and test mitigations now, then update those as systems become more capable. But it also limits the scope of the plan. If AGI turns out to work in a radically different way, some of that work may not transfer. So I’d view this as a basis for an evolving safety plan, rather than a claim that we’ve covered every possible route to AGI.

r001.rationale: It describes current systems as sufficiently similar to future ones, but does not define continuity in terms of smooth progress with respect to compute or labour.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the assumption does not mean progress will be smooth.

r003.rationale: It proposes investigating current failure modes and updating safety work, but does not say planning prioritizes problems at expected future capability levels.
